builder_plan.scenario: A multi-step product task fails because the agent loses track of dependencies.
builder_plan.change: Try the proposed planning step on tasks with checkable intermediate outcomes.
builder_plan.baseline: The same agent solving the same tasks without the new planning step.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Task completion, unnecessary steps, planning tokens, response time, and total cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Learning When Human Decisions Matter: Executor-Relative Consultation Value for LLM Agents
summary: The method replaces ad hoc escalation rules, direct prompting about when to ask a human, and rollout-based value estimation at deployment with offline Monte Carlo executor rollouts distilled into lightweight predictors for budgeted consultation allocation. It costs offline rollout supervision, executor-dependent value estimation, predictor training, and added allocation complexity, while avoiding rollout-based value estimation during deployment. It can fail when the offline executor rollouts do not match the production executor or task distribution, when the human budget or consultation interface changes, or when value predictors misrank rare but high-impact decisions.
rationale: The approach is implementable without large-scale infrastructure and targets a practical production problem, but its benefit depends on whether the reader operates agent workflows with costly human consultation and can validate allocation quality on their own executor and workload.

The paper states CVD improves allocation across five batch and three sequential settings with two frontier executors and broadly outperforms direct prompting and Value of Information where applicable, but the abstract provides no numeric factor.
